What makes selling a house in Reading, PA different?

Reading is a dense, rowhouse-heavy city where a sale needs a city Certificate of Transfer, carries a transfer tax of 5%, and often involves a house that has not been updated in decades. Those three facts shape price, timing and who is likely to buy.

Reading is the Berks County seat and the fourth-largest city in Pennsylvania, with 95,112 residents at the 2020 census. It sits on the Schuylkill River, with Mount Penn rising to the east and Neversink Mountain to the south. The Reading Railroad, the Schuylkill and Union canals and an iron industry that supplied Revolutionary War troops built the housing stock, and a good share of it still stands. Outlet shopping and pretzel bakeries remain part of the city's identity.

Sellers here usually weigh a repair-and-list route against a quick sale to an investor. The details below show what each route requires at the city and county level.

What do the Census numbers say about Reading's housing market?

Reading's housing costs are far below those of the Philadelphia suburbs, and most households rent, so the buyer pool leans toward investors and first-time owners.

With only about four in ten homes owner-occupied, a large share of Reading's houses are rentals. Owners of those properties also deal with the city's housing registration and rental inspection cycle, which can matter if tenants are in place at the time of sale.

What is the Certificate of Transfer in Reading?

It is a city document the seller must obtain before a property sale closes, and it applies to every property sold in Reading regardless of use. The City's Property and Codes Enforcement page states that the seller applies before the sale and hands the buyer a property packet with summary sheets.

A Health and Safety Inspection that checks code compliance is part of the process. Either the buyer or the seller may arrange it, and the city allows limited exemptions. The Housing Welcome Packet page lists the forms: a Certificate of Transfer and Property Sale Inspection Application, and a Property Sale Inspection Acknowledgement.

  • Download the sale application from the City's Housing Welcome Packet page and complete it as early as the sales agreement is signed.
  • Ask the City of Reading Property Maintenance division, which works from 815 Washington Street, for the current fee and processing time.
  • Agree in the sales contract who schedules the inspection and who pays for any violations it finds.
  • For help or complaints, the Citizen's Service Center is at 1-877-727-3234.

A seller who sells as-is to an investor should still get the certificate lined up. The document is the city's requirement, so it does not disappear because the buyer is paying cash.

How much transfer tax do sellers in Reading pay?

The Berks County Recorder of Deeds fee schedule states that the transfer tax rate is 5% in the City of Reading, compared with 2% in every other Berks municipality. One percent of that goes to the state, and the Recorder collects the whole amount when the deed is recorded.

On a house at Reading's median value of $121,300, 5% comes to about $6,065. Pennsylvania law makes both parties liable, so the sales agreement should say who pays and how it is split. Splitting it is a negotiation point, so settle it before the contract is signed.

  • Personal checks are not accepted for transfer tax at the Recorder's office, and cash is no longer accepted either.
  • The base recording fee for a deed is $88 for up to four pages, with $4 for each additional page.
  • A Statement of Value (REV-183) must accompany a deed that does not state the full price, and the Common Level Ratio printed on it is 3.12 for July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027.
  • The Recorder of Deeds is in the Berks County Services Center, 633 Court Street, third floor, phone 610-478-3380.

Certain family transfers and property passing by will or intestacy are exempt under state law, according to the Department of Revenue, so an inherited house passing to an heir may owe nothing.

Which Reading neighborhoods and roads matter to buyers?

Buyers sort Reading by neighborhood and by how quickly they can reach U.S. 422. The city's neighborhood map names areas such as Center City, Callowhill, College Heights, Hampden Heights, East Reading, Glenside, Millmont, Outlet District, Penn's Commons, Queen Anne Historic District, Prince Historic District and Southside.

The historic districts attract owners who want older architecture, while the Outlet District and Center City draw renters and investors. Reading Senior High School, serving grades 9 through 12, had 5,498 students in 2023 and is the largest traditional high school in Pennsylvania. Reading School District runs the city's elementary and middle schools, and Berks Catholic High School is a private option.

For commuting, U.S. 422 circles the west side as the West Shore Bypass, U.S. 222 bypasses the city to the west, Interstate 176 heads south toward the Pennsylvania Turnpike, and PA 61 runs north toward Pottsville. The city maintains about 132 miles of its roads, and the state maintains about 25 miles.

What about property taxes and assessments in Reading?

Reading homeowners are assessed through Berks County and pay the county, the city and the Reading School District. Ask Berks County for the current millage on your parcel rather than relying on a general figure.

Ask the Berks County Assessment Office for the appeal deadline and the form, because the rules for contesting a value are set at the county level. Ask the Berks County Tax Claim Bureau about any unpaid years. A title company will request a tax certification before closing, and unpaid taxes are paid from sale proceeds.

The city's code program adds its own tickets. Reading's Quality of Life program issues immediate tickets that increase with repeat violations at the same property in a year, and the city holds blight hearings for deteriorated properties. Clearing open violations before closing keeps them from becoming a buyer's negotiating point.

Should I list, repair or sell to a cash buyer in Reading?

The answer depends on condition and timing. A house in good repair near a historic district may do well on the open market, but a vacant rowhouse with deferred maintenance may be worth more to a rehab investor than to a retail buyer who needs financing.

  • Get a rough repair estimate before listing. Many Reading buyers use loans that require inspections and appraisals.
  • Work out your net after 5% transfer tax, the sale inspection, commissions and unpaid taxes.
  • If you own rental units, ask the Property Maintenance office how registration and open inspection findings transfer to a new owner.
  • If time matters more than price, a cash sale on an as-is basis avoids lender delays, though the Certificate of Transfer is still required.

More questions about Reading, PA

Is a Certificate of Transfer required for every house sale in Reading?

Yes. The City of Reading says the certificate is necessary for all properties sold in the city regardless of use, with limited exemptions only from the Health and Safety Inspection. The seller applies before the sale.

Who pays Reading's 5% transfer tax?

The law makes buyer and seller jointly liable, and the sales agreement decides who actually pays. The Berks County Recorder of Deeds collects it at recording and lists the rate at 5% in the City of Reading versus 2% elsewhere in Berks.

Can I sell a Reading house with code violations?

Yes, but the sale inspection will surface them, and the contract must say whether you repair them or the buyer does. Open violations that the city has recorded do not go away at closing.

Does an inherited house in Reading owe transfer tax?

Property passed by will or intestate succession is exempt from realty transfer tax under the state's rules. A later sale by the heir to a third party is a normal taxable transfer at the Reading rate.

Where do I record the deed after a Reading sale?

At the Berks County Recorder of Deeds, third floor of the Services Center at 633 Court Street in Reading, or by e-recording through a title company. Your closing agent usually handles it and pays the transfer tax by check.

How can I sell my house fast in Scranton, PA?

You can sell a Scranton house quickly by taking a cash offer, by listing it with an agent, or by selling it yourself, and the cash route is the one with the fewest moving parts. Scranton sits in Lackawanna County, and the city has its own rules for permits, rental licenses and transfer tax that can slow a conventional sale.

A listing in Scranton usually depends on a buyer's lender, an appraisal and a repair list. A cash buyer skips most of that, which matters when the house is inherited, has tenants, needs work, or sits on a street where older homes take longer to move. The trade-off is price: a cash offer is normally lower than a fully prepared listing, so compare both before you commit.

What kind of city is Scranton for a home seller?

Scranton is a hilly second class A city and the county seat of Lackawanna County, counted at 76,328 by the 2020 census, with a 2025 estimate of 75,514. That makes it the most populous city in Northeastern Pennsylvania and the sixth largest in the state.

The city covers about 25.4 square miles in the Lackawanna River valley. Inhabited ground runs from roughly 650 to 1,400 feet above sea level, with ridges on both sides, so lot slope, drainage and retaining walls come up often in inspections. The city is usually divided into nine districts:

  • North Scranton and Green Ridge
  • Central City and the Hill Section (Eastside)
  • Westside and West Mountain
  • Southside and Minooka
  • East Mountain

Green Ridge and the mountain neighborhoods read very differently to a buyer than the older streets near downtown, so a price from one district says little about another.

How did coal and rail shape Scranton's housing?

Most of Scranton's older housing stock dates from the anthracite and railroad boom. The Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad had its hub here and was the largest employer for nearly a century, and the borough became a city in 1866 after absorbing Hyde Park and Providence.

Population climbed from the 1860s until it reached a peak of 143,433 in 1930, then fell to about 76,000 as demand for coal dropped. The 1959 Knox Mine disaster effectively ended mining in the region. The housing left behind is large in number and old in age: narrow lots, brick and frame doubles, steep driveways and basements that have seen decades of freeze and thaw.

The city earned the nickname Electric City from a streetcar system that began running in 1886, and the neighborhoods built around those lines are compact, so houses within reach of downtown and the University of Scranton often draw a different kind of buyer than those up on the mountains.

What does the 3.7 percent transfer tax mean at closing?

On a Scranton sale the combined realty transfer tax is 3.7 percent of the value, compared with 2 percent in most of Lackawanna County, according to the county Recorder of Deeds. The Recorder will not take a deed for recording until the tax is paid.

Pennsylvania's own share is 1 percent, set by the Department of Revenue and collected by the county Recorder, with the rest going to local government and the school district. Who pays is a matter of the sales agreement. In many deals the seller and buyer split it, but the new owner is on the hook if the amount is ever questioned.

  • On a $120,000 sale, 3.7 percent comes to $4,440 in total tax.
  • Some family transfers, such as parent to child or between siblings, are exempt. Non-profit corporations are not.
  • A deed that shows nominal consideration, such as $1, needs a Statement of Value so the state can review it.

What are the key Scranton sale and rental costs at a glance?

Scranton figures. Sources: Lackawanna County Recorder of Deeds, PA Department of Revenue, City of Scranton rental licensing and code enforcement pages.
ItemRule or amount
Total realty transfer tax in the city3.7 percent of value
State share of that tax1 percent
Rental license, 1 to 3 units$45 per unit
Rental license, 4 to 9 units$150 flat
Rental license, 10 to 19 units$250 flat
Certificate of occupancy, new home$250
Rental license renewalDue March 15 each year

What if my Scranton house has tenants?

Every rental property in Scranton needs a city rental license, and renting an unlicensed unit has been a violation since September 16, 2023. Renewals are due by March 15 each year, and a new rental unit must be licensed within 30 days of a tenant moving in.

Fees depend on unit count, from $45 per unit for one to three units up to a $450 flat fee at fifty or more. Family-occupied units still need a license but pay no fee. Inspections run on a three-year cycle, and the first re-inspection is free.

If you plan to sell with tenants in place, have the license current before you list. A buyer's lender or an investor will ask for it, and a lapse can lead to refusal of a license, fines or worse. Ask the city's rental licensing office where your property stands before you pick a closing day.

What if the house is vacant, behind on its mortgage or heading to a tax sale?

Scranton requires registration of any property in the city, occupied or empty, that is in mortgage default, has a lis pendens filed, faces a foreclosure action, is subject to a tax deed application or pending tax lien sale, or has been transferred to the lender by a deed in lieu. Registration carries no fee, and it is done through the city's online portal.

The abandoned designation stays on the property until it sells, the foreclosure is dismissed or the default is cured. Selling before a judgment or tax sale ends that status, and a fast cash closing is one way to do it. Ask the Lackawanna County Tax Claim Bureau for the exact upset sale dates that apply to your parcel.

Do I need permits or repairs before I sell in Scranton?

Pennsylvania does not require a seller to renovate, but any work you start in Scranton needs a permit first. The city says all construction projects require one and no work may begin without it. Painting and gutter installation are the exceptions the city names.

Since January 1, 2026, plans have to follow the 2021 International Code Council series, with the 2024 International Property Maintenance Code applied to existing buildings. Three other checks catch sellers off guard:

  • Homes in a historic district or landmark need a Certificate of Appropriateness for exterior changes, even when no building permit is needed.
  • Projects in a FEMA flood zone go through the floodplain administrator, and a substantial improvement of 50 percent or more of market value triggers elevation or flood-proofing.
  • Fences, sheds and pools can need zoning approval even without a building permit.

Code Enforcement moved its in-person counter to 338 N Washington Avenue in October 2026. Open or expired permits on the house are a common reason a title company delays closing, so ask the office for the permit history before you list.

Should I worry about mine subsidence?

Possibly. Scranton grew over underground anthracite workings, and standard homeowner policies usually exclude damage from collapsed mines. The state's Mine Subsidence Insurance program, run by the Department of Environmental Protection, fills that gap.

Coverage runs from $5,000 to $1,000,000, and residential coverage of $150,000 costs $41.25 a year. DEP's MSI Risk map shows whether an address lies over mined ground, and a buyer's lender may ask. A policy does not transfer to the new owner, who has to apply for their own, and a seller who cancels at closing can get unused premium back when the notice arrives inside a month of the sale.

Cracks are sometimes soil settlement or frost rather than mines, and the program lists those as common look-alikes.

How does Scranton's winter affect a house that is for sale?

Scranton has a humid continental climate with 45.1 inches of snow in an average year, 38.72 inches of total precipitation and about 39 days when the high stays below freezing. January averages 28.0 degrees and July 73.7 degrees, measured at the Wilkes-Barre/Scranton airport.

That freeze-thaw cycle is hard on roofs, gutters, chimneys, retaining walls, concrete steps and old foundations, and buyers' inspectors look for exactly those items. A buyer who purchases as-is removes the need to schedule repairs around the weather.

How do schools and commuting affect Scranton buyers?

Public schools are run by the Scranton School District, which serves almost 10,000 students through two high schools, three intermediate schools and twelve elementary schools.

For commuters, Interstate 81 runs along the city's southeastern and northern edges, Interstate 476 (the Turnpike's Northeast Extension) sits along the west side, and U.S. Route 11 passes through downtown. Local buses are run by the County of Lackawanna Transit System. Several colleges sit in or beside the city, including the University of Scranton, Marywood University, Lackawanna College, Johnson College and the Geisinger Commonwealth School of Medicine.

More questions about Scranton, PA

How long does it take to sell a house in Scranton for cash?

A cash sale can close in a few weeks, since there is no lender underwriting or appraisal to wait on. The remaining steps are title work, payoff of any liens and recording the deed with the Lackawanna County Recorder of Deeds.

Who pays the transfer tax on a Scranton home sale?

The sales agreement decides, and in most deals the seller and buyer split it. The county Recorder says the state and local governments do not care who pays, only that the 3.7 percent total is paid when the deed is recorded.

Can I sell a Scranton rental property without a rental license?

You can sell it, but an unlicensed rental has been a violation since September 16, 2023, and the city can refuse a license or fine the owner. Apply for or renew the license first if tenants are in the unit, since renewals are due March 15.

Does Scranton require an inspection before I can sell?

The city's code enforcement and rental pages describe permit inspections and a three-year rental inspection cycle, and they describe no inspection tied to a sale. Ask the office whether anything is open on your address before you list.

Is mine subsidence insurance required when buying a Scranton home?

It is not required by the state, but a lender may ask for it when the property sits over mined ground. DEP sells the coverage, and the new owner has to apply for a new policy because the seller's does not transfer.

What should I know before selling a house in Radnor Township?

Radnor is a Main Line township in Delaware County with high home values, a mandatory township certificate for every resale, and a transfer tax that runs above the county default. A seller who plans around those three items can move quickly, whether the house goes on the market, sells to a neighbor, or goes to a cash buyer.

The township covers about 13.8 square miles and includes Wayne, St. Davids, Rosemont, Ithan, Garrett Hill and Villanova. It is home rule, run by a Board of Commissioners, and it was laid out in 1682 as part of the Welsh Tract. Lancaster Avenue follows the route of the 1794 Philadelphia and Lancaster Turnpike, and the Paoli/Thorndale rail line gave the area its commuter character in the nineteenth century.

Selling fast here mostly comes down to paperwork timing. Buyers, lenders and the township each have steps that can add days, and the sections below set them out in the order you will meet them.

What does the Census say about Radnor homes and owners?

Radnor is an expensive, owner-heavy market, and the figures below explain why pricing and buyer financing look different here than in much of Delaware County.

A median value above $800,000 means many sales involve jumbo loans, appraisal scrutiny and long inspection lists. About a third of households rent, so investors and landlords are a real part of the buyer pool near Villanova University and Eastern University.

Do I need a certificate of occupancy to sell in Radnor?

Yes. The township's FAQ confirms that use and occupancy permits are required for resales, and the Engineering Department issues them. No new owner may occupy the property until the certificate is out.

The Engineering Department's transfer page sets the sequence:

  • The seller files the application at least 10 business days before settlement. The owner signs it, and the fee is $150.
  • Filing 10 days or less before settlement triggers a $300 expedite fee.
  • The township inspects for house number display and public sidewalk condition, then sends a violation notice for anything that needs repair.
  • If sidewalk blocks cannot be replaced before closing, money goes into escrow with the department, and a sidewalk permit is needed for the work.
  • Sellers and buyers both sign a smoke detector and carbon monoxide certification, and the application is not accepted unless the form, the fee and the signed application arrive together.
  • The owner books an inside look at the sanitary sewer soil pipe to confirm there are no illegal connections, and sump pumps must be disconnected from the sanitary system under Chapter 235 of the township code.

Call the Engineering Department at 610-688-5600, extension 129, to book the sewer appointment. Do it the day you file, because that appointment is the step most likely to push a closing date.

How much is the transfer tax when I sell in Radnor?

Delaware County's Recorder of Deeds lists the state share at 1% and the local share at 1%, with Radnor Township named as an exception at 1.5%. On a sale at the median value above, each additional half percent of local tax is about $4,200, so confirm the exact split with the Recorder before you set a net-proceeds number.

The Pennsylvania Department of Revenue explains that the county Recorder collects the state's 1% along with any local tax. Both the seller (grantor) and the buyer (grantee) are jointly liable, which is why a sales agreement states who pays. Certain transfers between family members, and property passed by will or intestate succession, are exempt under state rules, so an inherited house moving to an heir is treated differently from a market sale.

The county's recording office is at the Government Center in Media, and its transfer tax page lists the state's Statement of Value form (REV-183) for deeds that do not state full consideration. If a deed leaves the price off, that form is what carries the value to the Recorder.

When are Radnor property taxes due, and how do appeals work?

Township bills go out on or before February 1, and the face amount is due May 31. According to the township's FAQ, paying by March 31 earns a 2% discount, and a 10% penalty applies after May 31. The Radnor School District bills and collects its own tax separately, with school bills mailed in July.

An unpaid bill becomes a lien if it is not paid by the end of the calendar year, and the Delaware County Tax Claim Bureau adds interest and penalties. When a house sells, the township asks that you return the bill with the new owner's name, because the Recorder can take more than 60 days to process a title transfer.

  • Assessment appeals go to the Delaware County Board of Assessment Appeals before August 1 for a value effective the following January 1.
  • An appeal does not pause the bill. You pay what is billed and receive a refund or credit if the value drops.
  • The county reassessment that ran from December 2017 to 2020 took effect in January 2021, so current values reflect that base year.
  • A tax certification from the township finance office costs $25 per parcel, and title companies typically request one.

Sewer and stormwater are billed together on a separate mailing around April 1, due May 31. The stormwater charge depends on parcel size, and it applies to all developed properties in the township.

Which neighborhoods and schools affect a Radnor sale?

Schools drive demand more than any other local factor. Public students attend the Radnor Township School District, which runs Radnor High School, Radnor Middle School, and Radnor, Ithan and Wayne elementary schools. Private options inside the township include Archbishop John Carroll High School, the Agnes Irwin School, the Hill Top Preparatory School and the Valley Forge Military Academy and College.

Buyer groups differ by area. Downtown Wayne has historic districts, with North Wayne and South Wayne as residential pockets around a commercial core. St. Davids and Ithan are quieter residential neighborhoods, while Villanova and Garrett Hill have long-standing Catholic parish communities. Strafford, Bryn Mawr and Villanova straddle township lines, so a listing's mailing address may not match its municipality, and that matters for transfer tax and the certificate.

Commuting helps resale. The township has SEPTA Regional Rail stops at Wayne, St. Davids, Radnor and Villanova, plus seven Norristown High Speed Line stations. U.S. 30 runs along Lancaster Avenue, Route 320 follows Sproul and Spring Mill Roads, and Interstate 476 meets U.S. 30 inside the township.

Which selling route fits a Radnor house?

Three paths cover most sellers, and each handles the township certificate differently.

  • A traditional listing suits houses in good repair. The agent coordinates the certificate, but showings, inspection requests and buyer financing set the schedule.
  • A for-sale-by-owner sale saves the commission and leaves you running the certificate, the sewer inspection and the transfer tax paperwork yourself.
  • A cash sale to a company that buys as-is removes lender timing and repairs from the buyer side. The seller still files the township application and still schedules the sewer check, so ask any buyer who does the filing and who pays any sidewalk escrow.

Compare offers on net proceeds, not headline price. Subtract the transfer tax, the $150 or $300 township fee, any sidewalk or sewer repairs, and unpaid taxes before you decide.

More questions about Radnor, PA

Who applies for the certificate of occupancy in Radnor?

The seller does. The application goes to the Radnor Engineering Department at least 10 business days before settlement, signed by the owner, with the $150 fee and the smoke detector and carbon monoxide form signed by seller and buyer.

What happens if my sidewalk is damaged at the time of sale?

The township sends a violation notice after its inspection. If the sidewalk blocks cannot be replaced before settlement, money is placed in escrow with the Engineering Department, and a sidewalk permit is required for the repair.

Is Radnor's transfer tax higher than the rest of Delaware County?

Yes. The county's Recorder of Deeds shows most municipalities at the 1% default local share and lists Radnor Township at 1.5%, plus the 1% state tax. Ask the Recorder to confirm the combined figure for your deed.

Can I sell a Radnor house that needs repairs?

Yes, but the sewer connection, sidewalk and house number items flagged by the township still have to be corrected or escrowed before the certificate is released. Cosmetic and structural repairs are a matter between you and the buyer.

Where do I get a Radnor tax certification for closing?

From the Radnor Township finance office at 301 Iven Avenue in Wayne. The township charges $25 per certification, and you need the parcel (folio) number, the owner name and the address.

The school district and the township can appeal an assessment too. Commercial districts cluster along McKnight Road, U.S. Route 19 (Perry Highway) and Babcock Boulevard.

What should a seller know about Ridley Township, PA?

Ridley Township is a compact, mostly built-out suburb in southeastern Delaware County where owners are long-settled and the housing stock is older. A sale here depends on a short call to the township's Code Enforcement office, the county's 1% local transfer tax default, and a buyer pool that is mostly local.

The township covers about 5.1 square miles of land, with more water along the Delaware River at its southern edge. It includes the communities of Folsom, Woodlyn, Crum Lynne and Holmes, plus parts of Morton and Secane. Rutledge Borough sits entirely inside Ridley's boundaries, and Ridley Park Borough is surrounded on three sides by the township, so the municipal line is not always obvious from a street address.

Ridley was named for Ridley in Cheshire, England, and its tax collectors were appointed as early as 1684. Continental Army troops camped along its roads after the Battle of Brandywine in 1777, and the township grew sharply after World War II, from about 8,600 residents in 1940 to nearly 36,000 by 1960.

What do Census figures show about Ridley homes?

What does Ridley Township require when I sell my home?

Call the Code Enforcement office before you go to settlement. The township's code page says plainly that sellers should contact it for the necessary information, and the phone number is 610-534-4803.

The page also notes that owners of rental units must hold an annual certificate of use for each dwelling unit, whether occupied or empty. If you are selling a duplex or a house that was rented, confirm that the certificate is current so it does not become a closing problem.

  • Ask which inspections or forms the township wants for a sale at your address.
  • Ask whether any open violations, stormwater issues or unpermitted work are on file.
  • Ask for the township's current fee list, since permit and certificate charges are set locally.
  • Keep sidewalks and shared driveways clear of snow and ice within 24 hours after snow stops, because the township enforces that rule and buyers walking a property in winter will notice.

The township also publishes its code book, zoning map and a stormwater management ordinance, which matter if a buyer plans an addition or paving.

How much is transfer tax on a Ridley sale?

Delaware County's Recorder of Deeds lists a default of 1% to the state and 1% to the local municipality, and Ridley Township is not among the exceptions it names. Radnor, Upper Darby, Upper Providence and Chester are the ones that pay more.

At the Census median value of $265,200, 1% is about $2,650, so the combined 2% comes to roughly $5,300. The Pennsylvania Department of Revenue says both parties are jointly liable and that some transfers, such as certain family transfers and property passing through an estate, are exempt. The contract should still say who pays.

  • The Recorder of Deeds is in Room 108 of the Government Center at 201 West Front Street in Media, phone 610-891-4152.
  • Recording hours are 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., a full hour before the 4:30 p.m. office close.
  • Ask your closing agent how the recording fee and the two taxes are paid, because the office takes them separately.
  • If the deed does not state the full price, the state's Statement of Value (REV-183) goes with it.

Because deeds for several municipalities are filed in the same office, check that your deed names Ridley Township as the municipality. A mistake there changes the local tax line.

Which schools, roads and neighborhoods shape demand in Ridley?

Students living in the township generally attend the Ridley School District, and Our Lady of Angels Regional School, which formed in 2012 from two parish schools, is the nearby Catholic option. Families searching in this area often use the district as a filter, so a listing's school assignment is worth stating in the first lines.

Access is a selling point. Interstate 95 crosses the southern part of the township, Interstate 476 begins at I-95 and runs northwest across the southwest corner, U.S. 13 follows Chester Pike, PA 291 follows Industrial Highway and PA 420 follows Kedron Avenue. SEPTA city bus route 37 and suburban routes 113 and 114 serve the township. The nearest regional rail stations are in neighboring municipalities, since the Media/Wawa and Wilmington/Newark lines only clip the edges.

The township maintains about 72 miles of road, and PennDOT maintains about 14 miles.

How do property taxes and assessments work for a Ridley seller?

Ridley homeowners pay Delaware County, Ridley Township and the Ridley School District, each on its own bill. Ask the Delaware County Assessment Office for the current appeal deadline and form, and ask the township treasurer for the township's tax certification before closing.

Delaware County's countywide reassessment took effect in January 2021, so values across the county were reset at the same base year. A seller who thinks the assessed value is out of line can appeal, but filing an appeal does not stop the bill from coming due.

Stormwater is its own cost. Ridley adopted a stormwater management ordinance, last updated in September 2022, and publishes a stormwater fee schedule on its code page. Ask the township how the fee is billed on your parcel and whether any credit applies.

Which way to sell is best in Ridley?

A listing makes sense when the house is updated and priced against recent nearby sales. A cash sale works better when the house is dated, an estate is involved or the owner has to move on a deadline.

  • For a tenant-occupied house, confirm the annual certificate of use and the lease terms.
  • For a quick sale, ask the buyer to put the closing date and who pays transfer tax in writing.

Whichever route you choose, gather the tax bills, the deed and any township notices before you call anyone. With 73.7% of Ridley homes owner-occupied and few households moving in a given year, a clean file and a firm closing date set one offer apart from another.

Call the Code Enforcement office at 610-534-4803 to find out. The township's own page tells sellers to contact that office for the necessary information before settlement, so the answer for your address comes from them.

Students living in the township generally attend the Ridley School District. Parts of Morton and Secane lie inside the township, so check the school district on your tax bill.

How do I sell my house fast in Spring Township, PA?

A direct cash sale is the fastest route for a Spring Township house, but the township's property transfer inspection has to be scheduled either way. Spring Township is in Berks County, west of Reading, and it requires an exterior inspection of every single and multiple family dwelling before title changes hands.

The inspection is the step that most often decides the calendar, so this page puts it first and then covers the township itself: where it sits, what its housing looks like in Census figures, how the creeks and hills affect lots, and what the buyer and seller each pay.

What is the Spring Township property transfer inspection?

It is a required exterior check under the township's Property Transfer Ordinance 341, in effect since August 1, 2007, and the Code Enforcement Officer must inspect before title transfers. The seller, buyer or either side's agent can file the application.

The application goes to the Code and Zoning Office no later than 30 business days before settlement. The fee is $150 per property, and it rises to $250 if the application arrives fewer than 15 business days before settlement. After a complete application, the officer inspects within 10 business days.

  • Utility and storm drainage easements and road rights-of-way must be clear of obstructions, including landscaping.
  • Fences, pools, spas, sheds and decks must be permitted and sit within setback and yard rules. Pool fencing needs a self-closing, latching gate.
  • Sanitary sewer connections must control inflow and infiltration, and sump pump discharge must be properly placed.
  • The number of dwelling units, bedrooms and smoke detectors is checked against township records.

How much does the inspection cost and how long does it take?

The inspection covers only exterior, observable conditions, and nobody has to be home as long as the inspector can reach the backyard. Add a note with a phone number to the application if you want to be there.

What happens if the inspection finds problems?

Seller and buyer both sign the report to confirm they read it and agree to correct what it lists, and the township then issues a Property Transfer Certificate once the deficiencies are done. That can happen before or after settlement.

You do not have to fix everything before closing. If the buyer is willing to take on the repairs, an addendum to the agreement of sale normally settles who is responsible and how the money works. The township suggests ordering the inspection soon after you decide to sell, because the report has to be disclosed to the buyer and an early look leaves time to permit anything that was built without approval.

Common findings are an unpermitted shed or deck, a fence in an easement, or a pool without the right barrier. Those are fixable, and a cash buyer who plans to renovate will often accept them as part of an as-is purchase.

Where is Spring Township and what is the area like?

Spring Township covers about 18.4 square miles of land in Berks County, west of Reading and next to Wyomissing, Sinking Spring and Adamstown. The Census Bureau counted 28,407 residents in 2020 and estimates 28,873 for 2025, a gain of 1.7 percent. It is the second largest municipality in the county after Reading.

The township was split from Cumru Township in 1850 and takes its name from a large spring that appeared and disappeared with the limestone beneath it, which early settlers called the Sinking Spring. Terrain varies a lot: low ground in the north, with Cacoosing Creek on the northwest edge and Tulpehocken Creek on the northeast, and hills toward the Lancaster County line in the southwest. Communities inside the township include West Lawn, Whitfield, Spring Ridge, Vinemont and Montrose Manor.

Wertz's Covered Bridge, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1978, is one of the landmarks. The township shares the main western Reading retail district with Wyomissing, and Penn State Berks sits in the northeast corner.

About 17.6 percent of residents speak a language other than English at home, and 9.1 percent are foreign-born. Median selected monthly owner costs are $1,754 with a mortgage and $819 without. About a quarter of homes are rented, so some sellers here are small landlords who should check lease dates before setting a closing date.

How do the roads, bus routes and schools matter to buyers?

Spring Township has 130.6 miles of public roads, of which 112.16 miles are maintained by the township and the rest by PennDOT. U.S. 222, U.S. 422 and Pennsylvania Route 724 cross it, and U.S. 222 south gives expressway access toward the Pennsylvania Turnpike and Lancaster. Mean travel time to work is 23.6 minutes.

BARTA bus routes 12, 14, 15 and 16 serve residential and business areas and connect to the transportation center in Reading. Public schools are in the Wilson School District, which has five elementary schools, two middle schools and Wilson High School. For a buyer, a house near a bus line or the bypass reads differently from one in a quieter subdivision, so mention it in any listing or offer discussion.

Which township rules can catch a seller by surprise?

Spring Township reviews more than 700 permits a year and enforces its fence, shed and pool rules closely. Fences in a front yard are limited to 4 feet and must be open style, rear-yard fences can reach 6 feet, and sheds are not allowed in required front or side yards.

Residential grass and weeds may not exceed 8 inches. After a verified complaint the township sends a notice, cuts the property after 7 days if the owner does not, and bills the owner, and unpaid amounts become a lien on the real estate. Sidewalks must be cleared of snow and ice within 24 hours after it stops, with the same lien risk. Clear both before you list so the inspection comes back clean.

County and municipal tax payments can be made online through the Berks County Treasurer, and Wilson School District taxes are paid at Fulton Bank, according to the township tax collector's page. Call the tax collector's office for a payoff figure before closing.

Pennsylvania charges a 1 percent state realty transfer tax, collected with any local share by the Berks County Recorder of Deeds when the deed is recorded. Ask the Recorder for the combined local rate, and expect the buyer and seller to split it unless the sales agreement says otherwise.

What is the late fee for a Spring Township transfer inspection?

The fee is $250 instead of $150 when the application arrives fewer than 15 business days before settlement. The inspector still responds within 10 business days of a complete application.

Do I have to fix every item before closing?

No. A buyer can agree to make the corrections, and an addendum to the agreement of sale usually covers it. The Property Transfer Certificate is issued once the deficiencies are completed, before or after settlement.

The Census Bureau estimates 28,873 residents as of July 1, 2025, up from 28,407 in the 2020 census. It is the second most populous municipality in Berks County.

Which school district serves Spring Township?

The Wilson School District serves the township, with five elementary schools, two middle schools and Wilson High School. School real estate tax is paid separately from county and township tax.

Springettsbury Township sits east and northeast of the city of York in York County, and the steps that set the calendar are tax certification, payoff letters and title work.

This page covers what is particular to Springettsbury: its history and neighborhoods, the retail and industrial base around the York Galleria and Interstate 83, the two school districts that split the township, and the tax calendar that determines what the closing company asks you for.

What is Springettsbury Township like?

Springettsbury is a supervisor-manager township of about 16.4 square miles, home to the York Galleria mall and a large Harley-Davidson manufacturing campus. The Census Bureau counted 27,058 residents in 2020 and estimates 27,617 for July 1, 2025, a 2.2 percent increase.

The name comes from Springett Penn, a grandson of William Penn, and the township was incorporated on April 20, 1891 out of the northeast part of Spring Garden Township. It includes the census-designated places of East York, Pleasureville, Yorklyn and Stonybrook. East York was first developed in 1903, and the housing built there in the 1930s sits alongside postwar subdivisions such as Fayfield and Haines Acres and newer developments.

Codorus Creek forms the western and northwestern boundary and Mill Creek runs along the southwest. Major roads are Interstate 83, U.S. Route 30, Route 462 (East Market Street), Route 24 and Route 124.

What are the Census numbers for Springettsbury housing?

Census Bureau data for 2020 to 2024 shows 10,202 households, a 72.5 percent owner-occupied rate and a median owner-occupied home value of $243,900. Median gross rent is $1,339, median household income is $86,335 and mean travel time to work is 22.0 minutes.

About 85.8 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, and more than a quarter of homes are rented. Retail sales in 2022 were $1,356,251,000, or $50,118 per resident, which reflects how much shopping in the York area concentrates here.

Which school district is my house in?

Springettsbury is split between the York Suburban and Central York school districts, and your tax bills follow whichever one serves your address. The township tax collector bills school real estate tax for both districts inside the township.

That split matters when you sell. School tax is billed separately from the county and township bill, on a different date, and a closing company needs the right district and the right year to prorate it correctly. Look at your most recent school tax bill, which names the district, before you give a title company the parcel number.

The closing company asks the township Tax Collector for a Real Estate Tax Certification, which shows whether York County, township, street light and school taxes are paid, with the year, face amount, discount and penalty for each. What property rules does the township enforce?

Springettsbury employs a full-time Codes Enforcement Officer who responds to complaints about property maintenance. The township's property maintenance page lists the issues that come up most often:

  • Fences, pools, decks, sheds and patios built too close to a property line.
  • Signs of the wrong size, type or location.
  • Cars, RVs, tractors, construction equipment and boats parked on grass, plus abandoned or junk vehicles.
  • Weeds, tall grass, trash, uncleared sidewalks, dilapidated buildings and unsafe structures.

Owners are asked to correct a violation voluntarily, and a finding can sometimes be appealed to the Zoning Hearing Board. If a violation stays open, the township can pursue legal action and the District Magistrate can impose fines for each violation. Fix open notices before listing, or tell a cash buyer about them up front so the price reflects the work.

What happened to the big employers nearby?

Springettsbury has seen several large facilities change hands. A 101-acre Caterpillar plant operated here from 1953 until the 1990s, and the vacant site was sold in 2002 and redeveloped as the York Business Center. The McCrory Stores headquarters was in the township from 1963 until the chain closed in 2002, and Bon-Ton Stores closed its township headquarters in August 2018.

More recently construction of a Post Consumer Brands logistics center on the Harley-Davidson campus finished in January 2017, and Hollywood Casino York opened in August 2021. For a homeowner, these shifts matter mostly through job access and traffic on Market Street and Route 30.

The state realty transfer tax is 1 percent of value, and local governments can add a share, with the York County Recorder of Deeds collecting it at recording. Certain family transfers and property passed by will or intestate succession are among the exemptions the Department of Revenue lists.

Ask the Recorder of Deeds for the combined local rate for Springettsbury and for current recording fees, then subtract both from your estimate of net proceeds. The sales agreement decides who pays, though both buyer and seller are legally liable if the tax is not paid.

Get at least one cash offer in writing, then compare it with the net from a listing after commission, repair credits and the carrying cost of waiting.

Ask any buyer who covers the tax certification fee, the sewer certification and the recording costs, and ask for the closing date in writing.

The fee is $20, paid by check to the Springettsbury Township Tax Collector. The closing company sends the request form with the parcel number, owner, buyer and settlement date.

Which school districts serve Springettsbury Township?

York Suburban and Central York both serve parts of the township. Their tax bills go out July 1 for York Suburban and July 15 for Central York.

Delinquent taxes from prior years go to the York County Tax Claim Bureau at 717-771-9232. Current-year bills are paid to the township Tax Collector, who goes by postmark date.

What is Shaler Township, and where is it?

After World War II it filled in as a residential suburb, which is why most of its housing is mid-century. Several Pittsburgh mailing addresses fall inside the township, and the area is served by the Shaler Area School District.

The terrain is hilly and cut by three stream valleys that drain north to the Allegheny River: Pine Creek, Little Pine Creek and Girtys Run. Neighbors include Hampton, Ross, O'Hara, Indiana and Reserve townships and the boroughs of Etna, Millvale and Sharpsburg.

What does the township require before I can close?

Shaler requires a dye test, a backflow preventer check and a final water reading from the seller, plus four township letters the closing company orders. The township says every document on its list is required for closing.

  • Dye test. The home must be tested to confirm that downspouts and rain leaders are not tied into the sanitary sewer. Results stay valid for three years. The township asks sellers to request the test at least 14 days before closing.
  • Backflow preventer. At least two weeks before closing, the seller contacts the Hampton Shaler Water Authority at (412) 486-4867 for a visit to confirm a dual check valve and thermal expansion tank are in place.
  • Final meter reading. Sellers and landlords schedule a final reading and send a copy to the closing company so escrowed funds can be released.
  • Trash account. Close the account with the hauler and leave the recycling cart for the new owner.

If the dye test fails, the plumber notifies the township and the owner. Repairs can go to any contractor, but the township's building inspector must be told at least 24 hours before work starts so the work can be inspected.

The dye test itself is paid separately. Three plumbers under contract with the township charge $30, $35 and $40 per test, and you may hire your own registered plumber if the dye test form and waiver go back to the township office.

How does the tax certification work for a Shaler sale?

For a sale or refinance, the seller gives the closing company three years of township and school district real estate tax receipts. The closing company may use those receipts or order a tax certification letter from the township for $50.

Property tax in Shaler involves the county, the township and the school district, so a bill can come from more than one place. If you have lost old receipts, call the township tax office at 412-486-9700 and ask for copies before the closing company needs them.

What are the transfer tax and recording steps?

Pennsylvania's realty transfer tax is 1 percent of the property's value, and local governments add their own share, all collected by the Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds when the deed is recorded. Both buyer and seller are legally liable for the tax, though the sales agreement normally says who pays it.

Some transfers are exempt, including certain moves between family members and property passed by will or intestate succession. If the house is part of an estate, ask the Recorder or the closing company which exemption, if any, fits your deed. Ask the Recorder for the current local rate for Shaler before you work out your net proceeds.

Does flooding or mine subsidence affect Shaler houses?

Both can, depending on the street. The township keeps FEMA flood maps on file and publishes zone maps for Girtys Run, Little Pine Creek and Pine Creek, which the township says flood periodically. The building and zoning office at 300 Wetzel Road will review the maps with you and help work out which flood zone a property is in.

Part of the township sits over land that was mined in the past. The Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection sells mine subsidence insurance because homeowner policies usually leave it out. Coverage of $150,000 costs $41.25 a year, and a buyer needs a new policy of their own because the seller's does not carry over. Sellers who cancel at closing can get unused premium back if they notify DEP within 30 days of the sale.

What does the buyer handle after closing?

Shaler buyers register for the 1 percent earned income tax with Keystone Collections Group and open a water and sewer account with the Hampton Shaler Water Authority, since both charges share one bill. They also set up trash service, which is mandatory under the township code and handled by the township's contracted hauler.

If the property will sit empty for longer than three weeks, the owner can apply for a trash waiver good for up to six months and renewable. A seller who knows the house will be vacant before closing should ask about it.

Is a cash offer a good fit for a Shaler seller?

It is worth pricing when the house needs work, the dye test or backflow check looks like a problem, or the family wants a closing date it can plan around. A cash buyer is usually willing to take on the township checklist, but ask who pays for the dye test, the $50 letters and any repairs before you sign.

Compare the offer against a listing net of commission and the transfer tax. If the gap is small, the speed may be worth it. If it is large and the house is in good shape, a traditional listing may still make sense.

More questions about Shaler, PA

Does Shaler Township require an occupancy permit to sell a house?

No. The township's Selling Your Home page states that occupancy permits are not required for the sale or refinance of a property. A dye test, backflow check and several township letters are required instead.

How long is a Shaler dye test valid?

Three years from the test date, and the township keeps the result on file. Request the test at least 14 days before closing so a failed result can be fixed in time.

Who orders the Shaler no lien letter?

The closing company orders it from the township for $50. It confirms that no municipal liens are unfiled against the property, and the water authority issues its own separate lien letter.

What is the Shaler Township population?

The Census Bureau estimates 26,833 residents as of July 1, 2025, down from 28,132 counted in the 2020 census. The township covers about 11 square miles of land.

Can I sell a vacant or inherited house in Shaler as-is?

Yes, as long as the township's closing requirements are met, because they apply to every sale. Notify the water authority if the house is empty so service can be shut off, and ask about the trash waiver while it sits.
